DIV: Diver or diverting. Indicates that an aircraft is being diverted from its original destination or flight plan due to operational, weather, or emergency considerations.
DLA: Delay. Used in ATC communications and flight plans to indicate a scheduled or unscheduled delay in departure, arrival, or en route progress.
DLY: Daily. Used in aviation scheduling and NOTAMs to indicate an event, inspection, or operation that occurs each day.
DME: Distance measuring equipment (DME). A radio navigation system that provides slant-range distance from the aircraft to a ground station, commonly paired with VOR or ILS for position fixing.
DNG: Danger. Used in NOTAMs and aviation warnings to indicate hazardous conditions, such as dangerous areas, military activity, or obstacles.
DNS: Doppler navigation system (DNS). A self-contained aircraft navigation system that uses Doppler radar to measure ground speed and drift angle for dead reckoning.
DO: Ditto. Used in aviation documentation and reports to indicate the same information as previously stated, avoiding repetition.
DOF: Date of flight (DOF). The calendar date on which a flight operation occurs, used in flight plans, NOTAMs, and operational logs.
DOM: Domestic. Refers to flight operations, airspace, or regulations that apply within a single country's borders, as opposed to international operations.
DP: Dew point. The temperature to which air must be cooled for water vapor to condense into dew; used in aviation weather reports (METAR) to assess humidity and potential for fog or icing.
DPI: Dots per inch (DPI). A measure of printing or display resolution used in aviation chart production and electronic flight bag display quality specifications.
DPT: Depth. Used in aviation to describe the depth of water on a runway, the vertical extent of cloud layers, or the depth of snow accumulation in field reports.
DR: Dead reckoning (DR). A navigation method that estimates an aircraft's current position by advancing a known position using course, speed, time, and wind correction.
DRG: During. Used in NOTAMs and aviation instructions to specify the time frame or period in which a condition or restriction applies.
DS: Dust storm. A meteorological phenomenon in which strong winds lift large quantities of dust, reducing visibility to less than 1000 meters; reported in METAR as DS.
DSB: Double sideband (DSB). A radio transmission mode in which both the upper and lower sidebands are transmitted, used in some aviation communication and navigation systems.
DT: Datum. A reference point, line, or surface used as a basis for navigation calculations, altitude measurements, or geographical coordinate systems in aviation.
DTHR: Displaced threshold (DTHR). A runway threshold that is not at the physical beginning of the runway; used for obstacle clearance, noise abatement, or taxiway considerations.
DTRT: Deteriorate or deteriorating. Used in aviation weather reports (SPECI, METAR) and NOTAMs to indicate worsening conditions such as decreasing visibility, lowering ceilings, or degrading system performance.
DTW: Dual tandem wheels. A landing gear configuration with two sets of dual wheels arranged in tandem on each main gear strut, used on heavier aircraft to distribute weight.
DU: Dust. Particulate matter suspended in the air; reported in aviation weather observations when dust reduces visibility or creates a hazard.
DUC: Dense upper cloud (DUC). A thick cloud layer at high altitude that can obscure visibility, affect satellite navigation, and produce icing or turbulence conditions.
DUR: Duration. The length of time a condition, restriction, or flight phase is expected to last; used in NOTAMs and flight planning.
DVOR: Doppler VOR (DVOR). A type of VOR ground station that uses the Doppler effect to improve bearing accuracy and reduce siting errors compared to conventional VOR.
DW: Dual wheels. A landing gear configuration with two wheels mounted side by side on a single strut, used to distribute aircraft weight on the pavement.
DZ: Drizzle. Light, uniform precipitation consisting of fine water droplets less than 0.5 mm in diameter; reported in METAR as DZ and associated with low-visibility conditions.
E: East. The cardinal direction at 90 degrees on the compass; used in navigation, runway designators, wind direction reports, and ATC instructions.
EAT: Expected approach time (EAT). The time at which ATC expects an arriving aircraft to begin its approach procedure; used for sequencing arrivals in busy terminal areas.
EB: Eastbound. A direction of flight or routing toward the east, used in ATC clearances, flight plans, and airspace designations.
ECHO: Echo area. A region on a radar display where reflected signals (echoes) from precipitation, terrain, or aircraft are observed; used by ATC for weather avoidance and traffic identification.
EDA: Elevation differential area (EDA). A defined area where significant changes in terrain elevation affect aircraft performance, obstacle clearance, or approach procedures.
EET: Estimated elapsed time (EET). The estimated time required to travel between two points along a flight route, used in flight plans and oceanic tracking.
EFC: Expect further clearance (EFC). An ATC advisory indicating the time at which a pilot can expect to receive additional clearance, commonly used during holding or ground delays.
ELEV: Elevation. The vertical distance of a point, terrain, or obstacle above mean sea level (MSL); used in airport data, approach charts, and obstacle clearance calculations.
ELR: Extra long range (ELR). A classification of aircraft or navigation capability enabling extended flight distances beyond standard long-range operations.
ELT: Emergency locator transmitter (ELT). An aircraft-mounted beacon that automatically activates on impact to transmit a distress signal on 121.5 MHz and 406 MHz for search and rescue.
EM: Emission. The transmission of radio frequency energy from aviation communication, navigation, or surveillance equipment; also refers to engine exhaust emissions.
EMERG: Emergency. A situation involving imminent danger to aircraft, persons, or property requiring immediate assistance from ATC or other aviation services.
ENE: East-northeast (ENE). The compass direction at 67.5 degrees, midway between east and northeast; used in wind direction, navigation, and ATC instructions.
ENG: Engine. The powerplant of an aircraft, including piston, turboprop, turbofan, or jet engines; referenced in performance calculations, emergency procedures, and maintenance reports.
ENR: En route. The phase of flight between departure and arrival, typically conducted on established airways or ATC-assigned routes above the terminal area.
EOBT: Estimated off-block time (EOBT). The estimated time at which an aircraft will begin moving from its parking stand, used in flight plan filing and ATC slot coordination.
EOD: End of data (EOD). A notation used in automated aviation messages, data feeds, and NOTAM sequences to indicate that no further information follows.
EQPT: Equipment (EQPT). Refers to aircraft systems, navigation aids, communication gear, or ground support equipment; used in flight plan fields and NOTAMs to indicate capability or serviceability.
ESE: East-southeast (ESE). The compass direction at 112.5 degrees, midway between east and southeast; used in wind direction, navigation, and ATC instructions.
EST: Estimated (EST). A calculated approximation of a time, position, or value used in flight planning, position reporting, and ATC coordination.
ETD: Estimated time of departure (ETD). The estimated time an aircraft will depart from the gate or take off from the runway, used in flight plans and airport coordination.
ETE: Estimated time en route (ETE). The calculated time required to fly from one point to another along a route, accounting for wind, speed, and distance.
ETO: Estimated time overhead (ETO). The estimated time at which an aircraft will pass directly over a specified navigation fix or waypoint.
ETS: Estimated time of stop (ETS). The estimated time at which an aircraft will complete its movement, such as parking at the gate or stopping after landing.
